# Quiet Spaces Need Audible Boundaries

A sign that says “quiet study” cannot overcome a printer, a group room with an open doorway, and staff conversations at the same desk. People infer acceptable sound from what they hear around them, not only from posted rules.

## Map sound transitions

Walk from the entrance to individual desks at several times of day. Note where speech becomes intelligible, where chairs scrape, and whether doors close fully. A brief decibel reading can support comparison, but the character and predictability of sound matter too.

## Provide choices before enforcement

Place collaborative tables and calls near active zones, preserve genuinely quieter routes, and make alternatives visible. Staff can then redirect a conversation without treating normal activity as misconduct.

The companion wayfinding study looks at how a first-time visitor locates these zones; this note focuses on whether the promised acoustic difference actually exists.
